title: Segment Trees
summary: A recursive range-query/update structure supporting O(log n) queries after O(n) build, with lazy propagation for efficient range updates.

slides.markdown:
"What's the sum (or min, or max) of elements between index i and j?" is O(n) with a plain array scan, every single query. A **segment tree** answers it in O(log n) after an O(n) build, by precomputing the answer for a hierarchy of overlapping ranges and combining a small number of them per query — the same divide-and-conquer instinct behind every other O(log n) structure in this group, applied to range aggregation instead of point search.

The payoff is bigger than a plain range-sum array (prefix sums also answer range-sum in O(1), no tree needed) — segment trees additionally support **point and range updates** in O(log n), which a prefix-sum array can't do without rebuilding.

slides.subTitle: Each node owns a range, split at the midpoint
slides.markdown:
Each segment tree node represents a contiguous range `[lo, hi]` of the original array and stores the aggregate (sum, min, max — whatever the problem needs) over that range. The root owns the full array; each node's two children own the left half `[lo, mid]` and right half `[mid+1, hi]`, recursively, down to leaves that each own a single index.

A node's stored value is always derivable from its two children — sum is the sum of both children's sums, min is the smaller of both children's mins — which is exactly what makes both building the tree and updating it a bottom-up combination process, no different in spirit from the post-order height computation from earlier in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: Building and querying a segment tree
slides.markdown:
```python
tree = [0] * (4 * n)  # generous over-allocation for a recursive array-backed tree

def build(node, lo, hi, arr):
    if lo == hi:
        tree[node] = arr[lo]
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    build(2*node, lo, mid, arr)
    build(2*node+1, mid+1, hi, arr)
    tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]

def query(node, lo, hi, l, r):  # sum over [l, r]
    if r < lo or hi < l:
        return 0                # no overlap
    if l <= lo and hi <= r:
        return tree[node]        # total overlap
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    return query(2*node, lo, mid, l, r) + query(2*node+1, mid+1, hi, l, r)  # partial overlap
```

The query function's three cases — no overlap, total overlap, partial overlap — are the entire algorithm; a query only ever recurses into partial-overlap ranges, which bounds the number of nodes visited to O(log n) rather than visiting every leaf.

slides.subTitle: Propagating a single changed value back up to the root
Mid vs mid+1 that silently drop or double-count elements
slides.markdown:
```python
# BUG: both children include mid, double-counting it
build(2*node, lo, mid, arr)
build(2*node+1, mid, hi, arr)  # should be mid+1, not mid
```

Every split must partition `[lo, hi]` into exactly `[lo, mid]` and `[mid+1, hi]` — any index appearing in both halves gets double-counted in aggregates (sum becomes too large), and any index appearing in neither gets silently dropped (sum becomes too small). This class of bug is especially dangerous because it can pass small, symmetric test cases by coincidence and only surface on specific range sizes — always double-check the boundary is `mid` / `mid+1`, never `mid` / `mid` or `mid-1` / `mid+1`.

slides.subTitle: Deferring range updates until a query actually needs that subtree
slides.markdown:
A **range** update ("add 5 to every element from index 3 to 7") done naively means updating every affected leaf individually — O(range size) per update, which can be O(n) in the worst case, defeating the point of a log-n structure.

**Lazy propagation** fixes this: when a range update fully covers a node's range, don't recurse into its children at all — just record the pending update in a `lazy` value at that node and update the node's own aggregate immediately. The children only get the pending update applied (and pushed further down) the next time something actually needs to look inside them — a query or a different update that only partially overlaps. This defers work until it's actually needed, the same laziness principle that shows up in lazy deletion for heaps or copy-on-write data structures.

```python
lazy = [0] * (4 * n)

def push_down(node, lo, hi):
    if lazy[node]:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        for child, clo, chi in [(2*node, lo, mid), (2*node+1, mid+1, hi)]:
            tree[child] += lazy[node] * (chi - clo + 1)
            lazy[child] += lazy[node]
        lazy[node] = 0

def range_update(node, lo, hi, l, r, val):
    if r < lo or hi < l:
        return
    if l <= lo and hi <= r:
        tree[node] += val * (hi - lo + 1)
        lazy[node] += val
        return
    push_down(node, lo, hi)  # must push before recursing into partial overlap
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    range_update(2*node, lo, mid, l, r, val)
    range_update(2*node+1, mid+1, hi, l, r, val)
    tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]
```

O(log n) per range update, matching point-update complexity — the lazy value defers the O(range size) work indefinitely, potentially forever, if no future query ever needs to look inside that subtree.

slides.sectionTitle: Segment tree vs Fenwick tree vs prefix-sum array
slides.subTitle: Pick by update frequency and query type
slides.markdown:
| | Prefix-sum array | Fenwick tree | Segment tree |
|---|---|---|---|
| Range query | O(1) | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Point update | O(n) (rebuild suffix) | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Range update | O(n) | O(log n) with a trick | O(log n) with lazy propagation |
| Beyond sum (min/max/gcd) | needs a different technique per operation | awkward — not all ops are invertible | works directly for any associative, combinable operation |

A plain prefix-sum array wins decisively if the data never changes. A Fenwick tree wins on code simplicity and constant factor when the operation is sum-like (or otherwise invertible) and only point updates are needed. Segment trees are the most general — the only one of the three that directly supports arbitrary associative combine functions (min, max, gcd) and range updates without special-casing, at the cost of more code and a larger constant factor.

slides.subTitle: Adapting the same structure for range min, max, or GCD queries
slides.markdown:
Everything covered so far used sum as the combine operation, but the entire structure works unchanged for **any** operation that is associative and has a way to combine two children's results into a parent's — min, max, and GCD all qualify directly. Swap `tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]` for `tree[node] = min(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1])` (or `max`, or `gcd`), and every other line of the build/query/update code is unchanged.

The one place this genuinely does change something: lazy propagation for a range **update** needs the pending operation to be correctly composable with itself (adding two pending +5 updates should equal one pending +10 update) and correctly combinable with the node's stored aggregate — for min/max, a range "set to value X" lazy update composes differently than a range "add val" one, so the push-down logic has to match the specific update operation being supported, not just the query operation.
